preamble: Fronting of the postalveolar/palatal affricate /tʃ/ to the dental-alveolar affricate /ts/ keeps the affricate manner and voicing and only moves the place of articulation forward. It occurs independently in several South Asian lineages: Kashmiri and other Dardic languages and Nepali (where the inherited palatal series is pronounced [ts tsʰ dz dzʱ]). In Europe the same change is the Chakavian 'cakavism' of Istria and several Adriatic islands, where č is replaced by c. In Polish dialects with mazurzenie (Masovia, Masuria, most of Lesser Poland, parts of Silesia), the older soft palato-alveolar /t͡ʃ/ (cz) merged with /t͡s/ as the series lost its palatalization, while the standard language and the other dialects turned it into retroflex /t͡ʂ/. Wikipedia dates this depalatalization to around the 16th century and says that mazurzenie may have originated in the Masovian dialect between the 14th and 16th centuries. For example, czas 'time' is cas in Far Masovian and Western Kraków speech. Wikipedia (Mazuration, after Dejna, Kuraszkiewicz and Rospond) says that in these dialects "the postalveolar sibilants merged completely with the dentialveolars", and Koneczna derives the merger directly from the depalatalization. In Kuryłowicz's account the archaic dialects, trying to adopt the neighbours' new retroflex /ʂ ʐ/, replaced them with the /s z/ they already had. For the affricates, English Wikipedia reports Kuryłowicz as saying that /t͡ʂ d͡ʐ/ then coalesced with /t͡s d͡z/, while Polish Wikipedia gives /t͡ʃ d͡ʒ/, both citing Milewski (1956: 49–50); since the other accounts derive the dentals directly from the palato-alveolars, the change is filed here as direct. A few mazurated forms entered the standard language, such as cudo 'marvel' and ceber 'bucket' for Old Polish czudo and czeber; Wiktionary already has cudo as an Old Polish lemma beside czudo. Old Polish had soft palato-alveolars (/t͡ʃʲ ʃʲ ʒʲ d͡ʒʲ/ in Wiktionary's transcription); they are filed here under the plain symbols.

examples.note: Turner's ċ marks the Kashmiri dental affricate /ts/ that regularly continues Old Indo-Aryan c (CDIAL 4655).
The Nepali reflexes of the Old Indo-Aryan palatal affricates are alveolar affricates: च [ts], छ [tsʰ], ज [dz], झ [dzʱ].
Spelled with the palatal letter च but pronounced with [ts].

In the non-palatal Chakavian of eastern Istria (Labin area), Bakar, Trogir and islands such as Vis, Hvar town and Baška on Krk, č [tʃ] is replaced by c [ts]. The from form zač is the conservative Chakavian pronunciation, which keeps č.
Pashto څ is /t͡s/ in the Kandahar and Quetta dialects and [s] in the northern dialects.
Wiktionary traces it through Proto-Scythian *čaθβāri and Alanic *čuββar, which still had *č.

languageExamples.language: Old Polish (mazurated forms kept in Standard Polish)

examples.note: Wikipedia (Mazuration, after Kuraszkiewicz 1972) lists cudo, cudny, cacko, ceber and dzban as mazurated forms of the standard language, "instead of Old Polish czudo, czudny, czaczko, czeber, dżban/czban". Wiktionary has both cudo and czudo in Old Polish and calls cudo "a result of Mazuration".
Wiktionary lists czeber among the Old Polish forms of ceber.
